en: Then, in a secluded place, the knower of Śiva, free from all attachments and with his external powers stilled, should perform the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga). || 1 ||
With divine flowers from Lake Mānasa, with unguents from Lake Mānasa,
as well as with incense, water offerings, oblations, food offerings, and sacred ornaments.
With variegated garments, lamps, and various canopies,
as well as with paintings and diverse banners, all fashioned by his mind alone.
With golden jars, ritual substances, and yak-tail whisks with golden handles,
one should commence the mental sacrifice to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Seated either in the lotus posture (padmāsana) or in the auspicious posture (svastika),
remaining motionless, one should make oneself and the mind Śiva-like within the heart.
Then, having meditated upon the god Śiva, who is perfectly established within the self of all,
the knower of the path should worship him according to the method taught by Anantavijaya.
Those seekers of the Self who worship the Lord according to this method truly cause those beings who have arisen from the ocean of Māyā to cross over to the state of existence.
Neither by deed, nor by mind, nor by speech have they ever been defiled;
because they have become the self of all beings, they have no fear of them.
For this water-pot is indeed the companion of those who are alone and unattached;
therefore, the rule for its disposal is said to originate from the mouth of the Lord of Death.
Having first smeared the water-pot with pure earth, ashes, and cow-dung consecrated by the five Brahmans, one should place it in a clean location.
Having consumed it with kusha grass and other materials while reciting the Aghora mantra,
one who has sipped water (ācānta) should then sprinkle it with water while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having washed [the vessel] and facing either the east or the north,
he should first fill the water-pot with water.
With the syllable Om, one should offer [the remains] first to Śiva and then to the Guru;
having sipped water, one should sprinkle oneself with water in an unconfused place by means of the splendor of the weapon-mantra. 13.
Then, having released that [substance] with that very hand, one should thoroughly cleanse both hands; for since another person is pure, one's own hands must indeed remain wet.
One who is impure shall not touch the deity, nor shall one who has not sipped water perform the pointing-out;
he should not entertain doubt, for he is pure in all ritual acts. 15.
O brahmins, this Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa], consisting of seven hundred and sixty-four verses, is now complete; may there be well-being unto you.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on the Mental Sacrifice, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṃgraha.
